analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to register cosmetics facilities, review ingredient safety, and force recalls of dangerous products.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan cosmetics safety bill with 11 cosponsors sat in the Senate health committee for 22 months without a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given the FDA real authority over cosmetics and personal care products for the first time in decades. Companies would have to register their factories with the FDA, list ingredients, report serious injuries caused by their products, and pay fees if they are large; the FDA could then review the safety of specific chemicals, set limits or ban them, order mandatory recalls, and require warnings on labels for children and pregnant women. It was introduced by a Democrat and a Republican together but never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use makeup, shampoo, lotion, and other personal care products would gain the most. The bill would require companies to prove their ingredients are safe, report serious injuries to the FDA, and give the FDA power to force recalls of dangerous products — authorities that currently do not exist for cosmetics. People exposed to the chemicals listed for first-year review (including formaldehyde-releasing preservatives and parabens) would get safety determinations with plain-language public summaries, and labels would carry warnings for children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups. State health officials would get access to facility and adverse event data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who use cosmetics and personal care products

how_it_helps.text: Under current law the FDA has almost no power over cosmetics — companies do not have to register, report injuries, or prove ingredients are safe before selling. This bill would have changed that by requiring facility registration and safety substantiation for every product sold in the U.S.

The FDA would have had to review at least five contested ingredients every year, starting with formaldehyde-releasing preservatives (diazolidinyl urea, quaternium-15), formaldehyde itself, propyl paraben, and diethyl phthalate, and issue binding safety orders — safe, safe with limits, or not safe.

The FDA would have gained mandatory recall authority: if a product likely causes serious harm and the company refuses a voluntary recall, the FDA could order distribution stopped, notify the supply chain, and publicize the recall to consumers.

Companies would have had to report serious adverse events — deaths, hospitalizations, disfigurement, serious infections, or hair loss — to the FDA within 15 business days, with records available to state health officials.

Labels and websites would have to carry warnings for vulnerable groups such as children and pregnant women, and consumers could call a contact number to ask whether a hidden ingredient (for example, inside a fragrance) is present.

The bill protected small businesses: firms under $500,000 in annual sales would not register or pay fees at all, and firms between $500,000 and $2 million would face shortened registration and be exempt from annual adverse event reports.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and distributors of cosmetics with more than $10 million in annual U.S. sales would pay registration fees to fund FDA's new cosmetics safety work. All manufacturers above small-business size thresholds would bear the cost of facility registration, safety substantiation records, adverse event reporting, and any ingredient bans or labeling changes, some of which would likely be passed to consumers in prices. Businesses under $500,000 in annual sales would be exempt entirely, and firms between $500,000 and $2 million would face simplified requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have preempted most new state cosmetic safety rules. States could not pass new ingredient standards while the FDA reviewed a chemical, and the FDA reviews only about five ingredients a year — so states like California could not move faster than Washington on chemicals waiting years in line.
The list of ingredients to be reviewed each year would be chosen in consultation with the cosmetics industry itself, giving the regulated industry a formal seat in setting the regulator's agenda.

The FDA could not deem an ingredient harmful merely because it causes minor or transient allergic reactions or skin irritation in some users, which would leave common irritation complaints outside the agency's reach.
Registration fees and compliance costs fall on manufacturers with over $10 million in sales and would likely be passed partly to consumers through higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers are large relative to the costs: cosmetics have been essentially unregulated at the federal level since 1938, and the bill would have created registration, injury reporting, ingredient review, and recall authority funded mainly by fees on large manufacturers. The most serious design flaw is the preemption provision, which would have traded state-level protection for a federal review process that covers only about five chemicals a year and lets the industry help choose which ones. Even so, on balance this was a consumer-safety bill whose main cost fell on an industry that currently faces none of these requirements.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee never took it up — no markup, no vote — and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 7, 2019 by Sen. Dianne Feinstein with Sen. Susan Collins as co-lead sponsor.
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.

The bill would have required cosmetics facilities to register with the FDA, given the FDA authority to review at least five ingredients per year (starting with diazolidinyl urea, diethyl phthalate, formaldehyde, propyl paraben, and quaternium-15), and authorized fees on manufacturers with more than $10 million in annual U.S. sales.
The bill would have given the FDA mandatory recall authority and power to suspend distribution of products likely to cause serious adverse health consequences.

The bill included substantial small-business carve-outs: firms under $500,000 in annual cosmetics sales were excluded from the definition of a facility, and firms between $500,000 and $2 million faced abbreviated registration and reduced record-keeping duties.

The bill would have preempted most new state cosmetic safety rules, freezing state requirements for registration, recalls, and reporting as of enactment and blocking new state ingredient rules while the FDA reviewed a chemical.
No committee action ever followed the referral, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The cosmetics and personal care products industry is better off: it avoided registration fees, mandatory recall authority, FDA safety reviews of contested ingredients like formaldehyde releasers and parabens, and adverse event reporting, none of which it faces under current law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large cosmetics manufacturers avoided new rules

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as principal Senate sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alongside Feinstein as co-lead sponsor.

for.name: Consumer and health groups (including the Environmental Working Group)
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and publicly championed cosmetics safety legislation; the bill's framework drew on proposals developed with input from consumer and health groups as well as the cosmetics industry, as reflected in the bill's consultation requirements.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the committee he chaired for the entire 22-month session without a markup, hearing vote, or report; no floor vote ever became possible.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a bipartisan effort — a Democrat and a Republican introduced it together, and its 11 cosponsors included 9 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — but it never reached any vote in the Republican-run Senate.

industries.industry: Cosmetics and personal care products manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have imposed registration fees on large manufacturers, FDA safety reviews of contested ingredients, adverse event reporting, and mandatory recall authority — costs the industry does not face under current law. The bill died in committee, so the industry avoided all of it.

The bill largely exempted makers with under $500,000 in annual sales and gave simplified requirements to those up to $2 million, but banned or restricted ingredients would have applied to everyone, including small brands.

The bill would have required fragrance and flavor suppliers to disclose complete ingredient lists to the FDA on request, ending a long-standing secrecy around fragrance formulas, but only when the FDA asked.
